In the field of reinforcement learning, experience replay has been a crucial component that facilitates off-policy learning and improves the robustness of algorithms. However, the current implementation of experience replay has a major drawback: it randomly samples experiences from the replay buffer without considering their significance. This can lead to a significant waste of valuable data, as less informative experiences are repeatedly selected over more informative ones. To address this issue, we propose a novel experience replay method that dynamically adjusts the sampling probability of experiences based on their variance of returns. This approach ensures that experiences with higher variance are sampled more frequently, thereby accelerating the learning process. Our method, which we call Variance Decrease based Experience Replay (VDER), has been successfully applied to various policy gradient algorithms, including REINFORCE, Actor-Critic, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). Experimental results demonstrate that VDER significantly improves the sample efficiency of these algorithms, with substantial gains in some cases. For instance, PPO with VDER achieves a 30% improvement in sample efficiency compared to the standard PPO algorithm. Moreover, VDER is computationally efficient and can be easily integrated into existing reinforcement learning frameworks. To facilitate the adoption of VDER, we have made our implementation publicly available on GitHub. This work provides a valuable contribution to the reinforcement learning community by offering a simple yet effective solution to improve the sample efficiency of off-policy learning algorithms. In this study, we introduce InDistill, a novel knowledge distillation approach that preserves data flow during model compression. Unlike existing methods, InDistill ensures that the compressed model processes data in the same manner as the pre-trained model, thereby facilitating the transfer of knowledge between models with different architectures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of InDistill through its application to a range of tasks, including image classification and object detection, where it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art knowledge distillation methods. sensitivity of quantum classifiers to disturbances and the existence of universal
adversarial instances that can deceive these models regardless of the input data.

In shared control settings, robots can assist users by taking control of specific aspects of movement, while still allowing for user input. This research explores how robots can effectively convey their intentions to users, enabling them to make more informed decisions about when to relinquish control. We examined two primary methods: visual cues and haptic feedback. We found that visual indicators can effectively inform users of the robot's control parameters, but may not accurately convey the robot's intentions. In contrast, haptic feedback provides users with a more precise understanding of the robot's control parameters, as well as its intentions. Ultimately, our results suggest that haptic feedback is a more effective means of communication in shared control settings. This research has significant implications for the development of shared control systems, particularly in applications where users must rely on robots for assistance. We hope that our findings will contribute to the development of more effective shared control systems, enabling greater collaboration between humans and robots.
